html:
The Gacaca courts were community courts set up in Rwanda to try people accused of taking part in the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. They worked from the early 2000s until they closed in 2012.

After the genocide, about 800,000 people had been killed and well over a hundred thousand suspects sat in crowded jails. The international tribunal in Arusha dealt only with leaders.

So the government revived an old custom. Gacaca means "short grass", the open space where elders met to settle local disputes. In the new version, elected lay judges of good standing heard cases in each community, in the open. Neighbours gave evidence, and those who confessed could get lighter sentences. Over about ten years the courts handled close to two million cases.

Supporters say Gacaca let survivors learn how relatives died, and let villages live side by side again. Critics such as human rights groups pointed to judges without legal training, weak defence rights and pressure on witnesses, and to the fact that crimes by the victorious army were left out. It is often compared with South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
sum: The Gacaca courts were community courts set up in Rwanda to try people accused of taking part in the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. They worked from the early 2000s until they closed in 2012.
